title: Alberta government to revise policy as school boards say new flag regulations could cost millions of dollars
summary: Alberta’s education and childcare minister says he will change an incoming school flags regulation that has school divisions collectively preparing to spend millions of dollars on hundreds of new…

image.caption: The Alberta government passed the Flag Display Regulation this fall, requiring schools to fly both the Alberta and Canada flags on separate flagpoles during the school year. (Collin Gallant/CBC)

blocks.text: Edmonton

Alberta’s education and childcare minister says he will change an incoming school flags regulation that has school divisions collectively preparing to spend millions of dollars on hundreds of new outdoor flagpoles.
Education minister says he'll change an incoming school flags regulation
Alberta’s education minister says he will change an incoming school flags regulation that has school boards collectively preparing to spend millions of dollars on hundreds of new outdoor flagpoles.

On Thursday, Education and Childcare Minister Demetrios Nicolaides told reporters at the legislature that school boards buying new flagpoles should “pause until we’re able to provide some additional direction."
Nicolaides has also said he believes the money would be better spent by directing it to classrooms.

A flag display regulation, made public in late October to accompany new legislation from last spring, says schools must fly the Canada and Alberta flags outside their buildings and on separate poles to satisfy national flag protocol.
The provincial regulation says any work needed to ensure the flags fly on separate poles is supposed to be done by Jan. 4, 2027.

items: New provincial flag rules will cost southern Alberta school board thousands of dollars, superintendent says

blocks.text: CBC News reached out to eight school divisions to ask about how many of their schools have just one flagpole and how much money they anticipated they would need to spend to satisfy the provincial regulation.

The Calgary Board of Education, the province’s most populous school division, counted 223 schools and leased sites with a single flagpole. Spokesperson Joanne Anderson said in a Wednesday email that the division estimated it would cost $4 million to install a second pole on every site. The regulation says that work is supposed to be done by Jan. 4, 2027.

items: New regulations on flags flown at Alberta schools to take effect in January

blocks.text: “We will not be able to meet the Jan. 4 outdoor flag installation requirement as we will need to procure and install the flags and flagpoles,” Anderson said in an email.
Calgary’s Catholic school division said 122 schools would need a second flagpole, and each pole could cost $20,000 to $30,000 to purchase and install.

In Northland School Division, which has locations across northern Alberta, 12 schools would need additional flagpoles, and each would cost at least $20,000, spokesperson Curtis Walty said in an email.
“Meeting the Jan. 4, 2027, deadline would be impossible,” his email said. “Installing additional flagpoles would place significant pressure on education funding.”
Edmonton Public Schools said more than 170 sites would need a second flagpole, and 77 Edmonton Catholic Schools would need a second flagpole. Neither provided cost estimates.

The Fort McMurray Public School Division plans to install wall-mounted flagpoles on some schools that cost $2,000 each as a temporary measure, before installing permanent flagpoles in the ground next summer, a statement said.
Opposition raises lack of consultation

The issue came to a head at a meeting of the Alberta School Boards Association (ASBA) in Edmonton earlier this week, where members passed a resolution calling on the government to suspend the flags regulation, restore school board authority over flag displays and eliminate the mandatory costs for installing flags and poles.
Smith attended a breakfast event with trustees in Edmonton Tuesday and held a fireside chat with ASBA president Shali Baziuk.

items: Alberta government to delay adopting new limits on flags at schools

blocks.text: NDP MLA Janis Irwin said she was at the meeting and heard the exchanges.

On Tuesday, she told reporters she believes the premier seemed to be unaware of the costs and challenges of installing flagpoles because her government fails to consult with affected people before introducing new rules.
“It should have been a wake-up call for her to recognize that she's making decisions without understanding the consequences on the ground," Irwin said.
Alberta Premier Danielle Smith speaks to the media in Calgary on Oct. 21, 2026. (Jeff McIntosh/The Canadian Press)
Baziuk declined an interview request Wednesday.
Smith was asked about the ASBA meeting in question period at the legislature on Wednesday.
"Admittedly, we didn't know that it is common to only have one flagpole at a school," she said.
Changes coming, minister says

CBC News requested interviews with eight school board chairs on Wednesday. Although all declined, Fort McMurray Public School Division chair Tim O’Hara said in a statement that he appreciated the premier’s willingness to listen and "her recognition that 'You don’t know what you don’t know,' as she stated in response to finding out how many schools exist with less than the newly required two flagpoles.”
O’Hara said the event highlights why meaningful exchanges with school boards are important to identify practical obstacles before the government introduces legislation and proclaims it into law.
Nicolaides also met with ASBA members in Edmonton, but on Monday.
On Wednesday, Nicolaides told reporters at the legislature he would be changing the regulations.
Education Minister Demetrios Nicolaides says he will review new school flags regulations after school trustees said hundreds of buildings need a second flagpole to fulfil the incoming rules. (CBC)
He said he would consider removing the requirement for the Canada and Alberta flags to be displayed outside schools, but didn’t have more details on what the changes would entail.
“We don't want school boards to be absorbing these kinds of significant costs,” Nicolaides said.
Flag protocols could dictate costs

Gary Komusi, a Calgary business owner who runs Signs Talk, installs and repairs flagpoles as part of his work. In an interview with CBC News, he said following national protocol around the Canadian flag prompts some limitations around how a school could fly a second flag.
For example, he said if the Canadian flag is flying alongside an Alberta flag, the Canadian flag must be on the left-hand side and on a taller pole.

The height of the pole each school requires would depend on what their existing pole is like, Komusi said. Once ordered, a pole could take six to eight weeks to arrive, he added, potentially making the Jan. 4 deadline impossible to meet.
Komusi said the cost would depend on the length of the flagpole and the time of year it is installed, but he estimates it would be at least $5,000 per flag.
Installers would have to pour a cement footing with metal components for each flagpole base, then erect the pole onto it.
Flags themselves aren’t expensive, Komusi said, but schools have to ensure the Canadian flag is the correct dimensions — twice as wide as it is long.
Komusi said he is sympathetic to schools that have to spend money to meet the requirements.

“I'm not looking at this as a windfall for Signs Talk, or the flag industry, which I guess it is, but it's a hardship on the schools,” he said. “If this all went away, that would probably be for the best.”
